title: Fenwick Tree: Count Inversions in an Array
oneLiner: Count the pairs i < j with nums[i] > nums[j] in O(n log n), using a Fenwick tree of seen values (or merge sort), and return it as a 64-bit number.
keyTakeaway: Scan left to right with a Fenwick tree counting seen values by rank. When you reach nums[j], the elements before it that are bigger form inversions with it: seen so far minus prefix(rank), the ones less than or equal. Sum that over j. The count can reach n(n - 1) / 2, about 5 * 10^9 for n = 100,000, so it needs a long in C#.
explanation:
An inversion is a pair of positions i < j where nums[i] > nums[j]: two elements in the wrong order. A sorted array has none, a reversed array of n distinct elements has the maximum, n(n - 1) / 2. Counting them measures how unsorted an array is; it is also how many adjacent swaps bubble sort or insertion sort would make, and it underlies ranking comparisons. Return the count for nums. Equal elements are not an inversion.

Checking every pair is O(n^2). Instead scan from left to right, keeping a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) that counts how many times each value has been seen. When you arrive at nums[j], everything in the tree came before it, so the inversions that end at j are the seen values strictly greater than nums[j]: j (how many have been seen) minus prefix(rank of nums[j]) (how many were less than or equal). Add that to the total, then add(rank, 1). Each step is O(log n).

As in Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, the tree is indexed by value, so first compress coordinates: sort the distinct values and map each to its 1-based rank. Values in the tests run from int.MinValue to int.MaxValue, so don't index by the raw value or by value plus an offset.

Overflow: with n = 100,000 the answer can be about 5 * 10^9, more than int.MaxValue (about 2.1 * 10^9). Return long in C# and accumulate in a long. Python ints don't overflow.

The other O(n log n) classic is merge sort. While merging two sorted halves, whenever the next element comes from the right half, every element still waiting in the left half is bigger than it and comes before it: add (left elements remaining) to the count. Interviewers accept either; the Fenwick version generalises to queries like "inversions with a value window", and the merge sort version needs no compression. Knowing both is the strong answer.

The visualization counts the 6 inversions in [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2]. Distinct values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are their own ranks here; the array shown is the Fenwick tree (cell 0 unused).

recognitionSignals: "How many pairs i < j have nums[i] > nums[j]?", or how far an array is from sorted.
Minimum adjacent swaps to sort, or counting how many people a runner overtook: inversion counts in disguise.
Pair counting over positions where an O(n^2) answer is obvious and n is large.
gotchas: The total overflows a 32-bit int for large n: use long in C#.
Equal values are not an inversion: count strictly greater with seen - prefix(rank), not seen - prefix(rank - 1).
Values span the whole int range, so compress to ranks rather than offsetting into an array.
In merge sort, add the count of remaining LEFT elements when taking from the right, and take from the left on ties (<=).
confusableWith: Fenwick Tree: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self (this track) wants the per-element counts; the inversion count is their sum.
Sorting: Merge Two Sorted Arrays (Sorting) is the merge step the merge sort solution counts during.

complexity.note: Compression sort plus one prefix query and one add per element, each O(log n). The rank map and tree are O(n). The merge sort solution is also O(n log n) time and O(n) space for its buffer.

referenceSolutions.python:
def count_inversions(nums):
    # Coordinate compression: each distinct value -> its rank 1..k in sorted order.
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}
    tree = [0] * (len(rank) + 1)  # Fenwick tree: how many of each rank seen so far
    total = 0
    for j, v in enumerate(nums):
        r = rank[v]
        i, at_most = r, 0
        while i > 0:  # prefix(r): seen values <= v
            at_most += tree[i]
            i -= i & -i
        total += j - at_most  # the rest are bigger and came earlier
        i = r
        while i < len(tree):  # add(r, 1)
            tree[i] += 1
            i += i & -i
    return total
